learningObjective: Enumerate factors that make a static analytical cost model differ from measured wall-clock runtime.
stem: Modern autotuning frameworks (Ansor, MetaSchedule, AutoTVM) use cost models to prune the search space before actual measurement. Which of the following make a static analytical cost model DIVERGE from the measured wall-clock runtime? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Register spills that are hard to predict from source-level operation counts; the true register allocation is decided later by the backend (ptxas, LLVM).
Cache and TLB hit-rate variability caused by neighbour kernels, previous benchmark iterations, or OS scheduling that a purely analytical model cannot see.
Warmup effects such as JIT compilation, lazy kernel loading, and GPU clock ramp-up that dominate the first few measurements.
The compiler's static model uses the same numerical precision as the target hardware; there is no divergence possible in principle.
Hardware-level effects (bank conflicts, MSHR saturation, memory-controller queuing) that are not represented in a purely analytical model built on op counts and shape dimensions.

explanation: Static analytical cost models operate on op counts, memory traffic estimates, and simple loop-bound arithmetic; they miss (A) spill decisions made later by the backend, (B) execution-context variability like cache pollution, and (E) fine hardware effects like bank conflicts and memory-controller queuing. Ansor's key contribution was to note that these gaps motivate learned or measurement-based rankings rather than pure analytical cost models. Option C describes warmup effects, which are a *measurement* concern, not a source of divergence between the model and the true underlying runtime — one runs multiple warmed-up measurements to remove them. Option D asserts no divergence in principle, contradicting the entire motivation of learned cost models.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: register allocation and spill decisions are made post-source and affect real runtime.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: cache/TLB context effects are outside a static model.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: warmup is a measurement-methodology issue, not a model-vs-truth gap. Once warmed up, the underlying runtime is stable; both model and measurement target the warmed steady state.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: precision alone does not close the model-vs-measurement gap.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: bank conflicts, MSHR saturation, memory-controller effects are not captured in simple analytical models.

assumptions: The analytical model is built on op counts, shape, and memory-traffic estimates only.
Measurements are taken after standard warmup and averaged/medianed.
nonImplications: Does not imply analytical cost models are useless — they are effective search-space filters.
Does not imply learned cost models close all gaps — they still approximate.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses measurement-hygiene concerns with model-vs-truth divergence.
distractorRationales.D: Denies the well-documented gap that motivates learned cost models.

performanceClaim.scope: Analytical vs. measured cost gap in tensor program autotuners
